1:
The two titles come from different things. Clarke and Keil both explain that the Greek and Latin named the book from its subject, the laws of the priests, while the Hebrew kept its first word, and he called; Keil adds the rabbinic names and describes the book as carrying to completion the law begun at Sinai, the spiritual statute-book of Israel. Ellicott presses that word for continuity, since it is one word in the original and ties this book to the end of the last, where the cloud covered the tent and the glory filled it; and he adds the synagogue's observation that the formula introduces the three great communications to Moses, from the burning bush, from Sinai, and now from the tent of meeting. Gill and Henry both notice a scribal curiosity, that the word's last letter is written unusually small. Gill reports the Jewish explanations: that God met Moses unawares, that it marks Moses's modesty in getting out of the way, or God's condescension in leaving heaven for a tent; Henry takes it to mean the voice was still and small, and contrasts the moral law, given with thunder from a burning mountain, with the remedial law of sacrifice, given gently from a mercy-seat.

Wesley asks why there had to be so many kinds, and answers three ways: some sacrifices acknowledged mercies, some satisfied for sins and some were mere exercises of devotion; the variety suited a people much addicted to outward rites, giving them full employment of that kind in God's service and keeping them from idolatry; and no single sort could represent at once the perfections of Christ, the benefits of his death and the duties men owe. Henry starts further back: it is taken for granted men will bring offerings at all, the very light of nature directing man to do honour to his Maker, and the rules exist lest men indulge their own fancies about sacrifice and, while pretending to honour God, dishonour him. Ellicott observes that the directions are addressed to the people themselves rather than given first to the priests to teach, and Gill that they were given to Israel and to no others. Calvin announces his method rather than his exposition: since much here has passed out of use and some he does not understand, he will keep to a brief summary, and let those who hunt for allegories have the praise they covet.

On what may be offered, Clarke begins with the word itself, from a root meaning to draw near: it is the gift by which a man gains access, like the present without which no one approaches a superior in the East. He narrows the terms, the herd meaning the ox kind and the flock sheep and goats, and observes that these are the very animals God told Abraham to offer, evidence to him that the patriarchs had an epitome of the law later given in detail. The contrast with the heathen is his own: they offered horses to the Sun, wolves to Mars, swine to Ceres and dogs to Hecate, whereas here every gross-feeding or ferocious creature is excluded, and fish because they could not be brought alive. Calvin makes the same restriction a rule of obedience: not every clean animal pleased God but only the domestic ones which allow themselves to be directed by the hand of men, deer and roes being sometimes tamed and still refused the altar. He gives two reasons for requiring a perfect victim, that the type must represent the complete perfection of Christ, and that the offerer must learn that uncleanness is repudiated. Wesley offers four reasons for the choice, among them that it brought the Egyptian deities into contempt to see them destroyed so often. Ellicott renders the clause more exactly; Keil notes that the burnt offering is called a holocaust because the animal was wholly consumed.
3:
The name is explained from one fact three ways. Gill takes the Hebrew from a root meaning to ascend, since the victim was not only carried up to the altar but went up in smoke, and notes that the Greek calls it a whole burnt offering because all of it but the skin was consumed. Clarke calls it on that ground the most important of the sacrifices, the only one wholly burnt; Wesley qualifies that every sacrifice was burnt more or less, and reads the totality as meaning the whole man was to be devoted, and deserved to be utterly consumed if God dealt severely with him. Ellicott explains why the ox comes first, as the costlier victim, and why the blemish matters: to offer a defective animal was an insult and a deception, which is what the prophet curses in the man who has a male in his flock and sacrifices a corrupt thing. Henry says the same from the offerer's side: he who considers God to be the best that is will give him the best he has, or he does not give him the glory due to his name. But he adds the caution that in Christ there is neither male nor female, and that no natural blemish of the body bars acceptance, only the moral deformities sin has introduced into the soul.

The words rendered of his own voluntary will are the crux, and only Wesley defends the English. Clarke says flatly that the Hebrew means to gain himself acceptance before the Lord, that all the versions took it so and the connection requires it. Ellicott renders the clause at the entrance of the tent of meeting shall he offer it, that he may be accepted before the Lord, supports it from a later chapter where for your acceptance is explicit, and observes that the phrase goes with burnt and peace offerings but never with sin offerings. Henry reports the same reading from Ainsworth, that the words give not the principle but the end of the offering, though he keeps the other sense too, since what pleases God must be done by no constraint but love, God accepting the cheerful giver. Wesley grants that on the received translation the passage speaks only of freewill offerings, prompted by supplication or thanksgiving rather than prescribed, then doubts his own gloss, since it seems improper to restrict to freewill offerings rules observed in the others too.

On the laying on of hands the witnesses are unusually specific. Gill gathers the rabbinic detail: the Targum says the right hand but the Jewish writers generally say both, and Maimonides requires a man to lay on with all his strength, on the head and not the neck or sides, with nothing between his hands and the beast, and with his own hand, not his wife's or his servant's. Ellicott confirms it from second-Temple practice: the offerer laid both hands between the horns while the animal was alive, no proxy could do it, and he preserves the confession said over it: I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed, but I repent before thee, and this is my atonement. Keil adds that the verb implies a forcible pressure, and that the rite is prescribed wherever the ceremonial is described minutely and passed over wherever it is condensed. Clarke enumerates what the gesture acknowledged, ending with the entreaty that God accept the life of the innocent animal in place of the offerer's own, and observes that almost every nation had burnt offerings and held that the gods could be appeased no other way, some going as far as human sacrifice on the maxim that only a life redeems a life. Wesley and Henry both make the transfer the point, and Wesley adds that the atonement here is sacramental, burnt offerings covering sin in general where particular sins had their own sacrifices.
5:
The chapter never says who kills, and the answers divide. Keil resolves it by distinguishing the cases: the offerer himself slaughtered in the private sacrifices, the priests and Levites in the national and festal ones. Ellicott has the sacrificer cut the throat on the north side of the altar while a priest holds a bowl beneath the neck. Gill leans the same way, since no one but the bringer has yet been mentioned and the traditions allow the killing to strangers, women, servants and the unclean; but the Targum makes it the butcher, Aben Ezra the priest, and the Greek turns the verb plural. Calvin alone denies the offerer any part in it: no private person might kill the victim with his own hands, and what the priest did in their name was transferred to them, since the pledge of reconciliation might be brought from home but the ministers of expiation had to be sought elsewhere, all hands being polluted but those God has purged. Wesley keeps both open, on the principle that men are commonly said to do what they cause others to do. On the blood they agree, and Ellicott is fullest: two throwings, from opposite corners so as to cover all four walls, and the rest poured out at the southern side into a drain that carried it to the Kedron.

The same question returns at the flaying, and Gill lays out the evidence without settling it: the verb is singular and seems to mean the bringer, Gersom allows a stranger to flay, Aben Ezra reads it of the priest, and the Greek and Samaritan make it plural. Clarke thinks the offerer probably killed, flayed, cut up and washed, then handed the parts and blood to the priest, but grants that priests and Levites flayed victims too, and that the red heifer alone was never flayed but burnt whole. Ellicott is definite that the sacrificer skinned and jointed it, the skin being the officiating priest's perquisite. About the fire there is a different puzzle. Clarke insists it was the fire that had come from before the Lord and was kept perpetually burning, no other being lawful, citing Nadab and Abihu. Ellicott confines the command to the first offering on the newly erected altar, since afterwards the fire never went out. Wesley reads the verb as disposing rather than kindling, blowing the existing fire up and putting it together. Gill reports the rabbinic tradition that although fire came down from heaven, fire was still commanded to be brought from a common place.

On the arrangement of the parts Clarke describes the operation: the head cut off, the caul taken out, the intestines and fat washed, the four quarters laid on the altar, covered with the fat, and the head above all. Ellicott insists the ordering was not casual, the verb meaning to lay in order, and reports the second-Temple rule that the pieces were arranged as far as possible in the positions they held in the living animal. Keil says the same of the wood. Wesley explains why the fat was gathered: to increase the flame and consume the rest faster. On the washing, Gill and Ellicott agree on the practice, three washings at least, and Gill adds from Maimonides that it must be water and not wine, then gives Philo's mystical reading, that the inwards meant lusts to be washed away and the feet that we should walk no more on earth but mount to heaven. Keil is more anatomical, restricting the term to stomach and bowels rather than the organs of the breast. All end on the savour: Ellicott notes that the word for burning properly means to raise a fume, Clarke that the Greek phrase is the one Paul takes up, Wesley that the smell was sweet not in itself, for it rather caused a stink, but as it represented Christ's offering of himself.
10:
The flock offering is provided for those who cannot reach a bullock. Ellicott says so plainly, that bullocks could only be offered by the wealthy and that the law now makes room for those unable to afford so costly a sacrifice; he specifies a lamb of the first year, which he says was the ordinary burnt offering in the time of Christ, rather than a goat. Henry sets the same point in a wider frame, that those of middle rank brought a sheep or a goat and those who could not manage even that were accepted with a turtle-dove or a pigeon, since God in his law and in his gospel, as in his providence, considers the poor. He adds why these creatures and not others: they were the mildest and gentlest, harmless and inoffensive, and so typified the innocence and meekness that were in Christ and that should be in Christians. Keil observes that the instructions already given for oxen apply here unchanged, which is why only the leading points are repeated, and Ellicott says the same, that the directions are therefore not restated at length. Clarke adds nothing of his own on the flock, sending his reader back to the note on the opening verses.

One detail is new, that the victim is killed on the north side of the altar, and the explanations fall into two kinds. Ellicott's is purely topographical: the refuse had its place on the east, the laver stood on the west and the ascent to the altar was on the south, so the north was the only convenient side left, and the same rule governs the sin and trespass offerings. Henry guesses similarly, that the largest vacant space lay there with room for the priests to turn in, and then allows himself a conceit, that fair weather was anciently said to come out of the north and the north wind to drive away rain, as by these sacrifices the storms of God's wrath are scattered. Gill supplies the measurements from Maimonides, a square of sixty cubits from the altar wall to the court wall which was called the north and reserved for slaying the most holy things, chosen as the largest place available. But Gill and Wesley both add a second reason. Aben Ezra, Gill reports, saw a reference to the situation of Mount Zion, which the psalm places on the sides of the north; and Wesley draws the same line, that the detail may mark the place of Christ's death, generally in Jerusalem and particularly on Calvary.

The rest of the section is repetition, and the witnesses treat it so. Gill says only that the flock was cut up in the same manner as the bullock, and the inwards and legs washed as before. Ellicott stops on one phrase, that with his head and his fat is loose English for a Hebrew figure in which a single verb governs two nouns though it properly suits only one, so that a second verb must be supplied: he shall cut it into its pieces, and sever its head and its fat. Henry uses the room the repetition leaves him to press the question of proportion. The offering of the poor, he says, was as typical of Christ's atonement as the costlier sacrifices, and expressed repentance, faith and devotedness just as fully; but we can no more offer the sacrifice of a broken heart than an Israelite could offer a bullock, except as God has first given it to us. And where providence has put much into a man's power, scanty offerings will not be accepted, since they are not proper expressions of a willing mind.
14:
The bird is the offering of the poorest. Gill notes it was for those who could bring neither bullock nor sheep nor lamb. Clarke turns the graded scale into an argument about mercy: the rich brought the costliest and the poor those of least price, and if a man could not manage even a turtle-dove, a little fine flour was accepted, bringing the sacrificial service within reach of the poorest. Ellicott counts five kinds, bullock, lamb, goat, dove and pigeon, the same Abram was commanded to offer, and adds that although birds were the concession to poverty here, in other cases they were prescribed for everyone regardless of means. He and Keil both explain the supply: turtledoves came into Palestine in large flocks at their seasons, and because of these sacrifices the Jews kept dovecots from time immemorial, dealers sitting with cages of them in the Temple court. Wesley gives a different reason for the choice, that the birds were easily got and represent the chastity, meekness and gentleness of Christ, and notes the one distinction of age: pigeons must be young because they are then at their best, while turtledoves are better grown.

What follows is unlike the rest of the chapter: the offerer drops out of it. Ellicott explains why: the priest himself carried the victim to the altar and killed it, probably out of consideration for a poor offerer's feelings and to give a small offering some weight; and the laying on of hands was dispensed with, the bird being too small for the gesture and the man having carried it in his own hands, which conveyed the same thing. Gill fixes the place at the south-east horn, near where the ashes lay. On the killing Ellicott is exact: no knife was used, the priest nipping the head off with his nails and throwing it on the fire; and since so little blood could not be caught in a bowl or thrown at four walls, he pressed it from the headless body and let it run down the side. Clarke describes the same sequence more roughly: the head wrung off, the blood poured out, the feathers plucked, the breast opened and the inner parts taken out. Wesley settles a possible confusion: the head was severed here because it was burnt by itself, and the rule elsewhere about not dividing the bird asunder belongs to the sin offering, not to this.

One phrase divides them. Gill reports that with his feathers is rendered with its meat, or its dung, by Onkelos and the Targums, meaning what was gathered in the crop, Gersom taking it to include the entrails. Keil argues the same way from the Hebrew: the Greek and Luther give the crop with the feathers, but the word would have to be a different one, and in any case the intestines would come away with the crop, so the Mishnah's account is substantially right without the feathers. Ellicott takes the opposite side on grounds of sense: as the skin was flayed from the quadruped, so the feathers must have been stripped, since one can hardly imagine them burnt and making an intolerable smell. But he concedes that most expositors now prefer the filth, and suspects two similar Hebrew words have collapsed into one. Wesley notes where the refuse went, on the east, the point remotest from the holy of holies at the west end, to teach that impure things must not presume to approach God. On the cleaving all agree the bird was split, not parted, and Gill alone reads it: the soul and body of Christ were separated in death, but the human nature was not divided from the divine Person, nor he from the Father who forsook him. Wesley ends where the chapter leaves him: to love God with all our hearts and our neighbour as ourselves is better than all burnt offerings.
